# What this vignette covers

In a distance-removal point count, the observer records how far away each bird
was and the part of the count in which it was first detected. Those two records
let a model separate how many birds were present from how many the observer
missed. This vignette shows how to estimate the scale of effect of a landscape
covariate on bird density inside such a model, fitted with
`unmarked::gdistremoval()`.

You will simulate a survey with known values, prepare the data, fit the model,
estimate the scale of effect, and read the abundance, availability, and
detection results. The last section lists what is not supported yet. Read
`vignette("v01-quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` first, because this vignette
builds on its four steps. Experience with `unmarked` helps but is not required.

# Know what data the model needs

`unmarked` stores a distance-removal survey in an `unmarkedFrameGDR` object.
A detected bird is removed from further counting, so only its first detection
is used.

| Input | Argument | Contents |
|:------|:---------|:---------|
| Distance table | `yDistance` | One row per survey and one column per distance band. Each entry counts the birds first detected in that band |
| Removal table | `yRemoval` | One row per survey and one column per time interval. Each entry counts the birds first detected in that interval |
| Distance bands | `dist.breaks`, `unitsIn` | Band boundaries starting at zero. The last boundary is the survey radius |
| Time intervals | `period.lengths` | Length of each interval |
| Site covariates | `siteCovs` | One row per survey, including the kernel-weighted landscape covariates |

Both tables describe the same birds, so the two rows for a survey must have the
same total. The model has four components, and each takes its own formula.

| Component | Formula argument | `type` | What it estimates | Link |
|:----------|:-----------------|:-------|:------------------|:-----|
| Abundance | `lambdaformula` | `"lambda"` | Bird density, or abundance per survey circle | Log |
| Availability | `phiformula` | `"phi"` | Probability that a bird is available during a visit. Estimated only when points are visited more than once | Logit |
| Removal | `removalformula` | `"rem"` | Probability, per unit of time, that a bird present is first detected | Logit |
| Distance | `distanceformula` | `"dist"` | Scale of the detection function, or how quickly detection falls with distance | Log |

`multiScaleR` estimates a scale of effect for a landscape covariate in any
component the model estimates. The example below visits each point once. Its
removal component therefore carries the information about how readily birds
reveal themselves.

# Simulate a survey with a known scale of effect

The running count example from the Quick Start does not fit this model, so this
vignette simulates point counts on the same landscape with `sim_dat_gdr()`.

```{r load-data}
data("surv_pts")                 # 100 survey locations (an sf object)
pts <- vect(surv_pts)            # convert to a terra SpatVector

# Binary habitat layer on a 20 m grid, in meters
land1 <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                          package = "multiScaleR"))[["land1"]]

# Step 1 of every analysis: extract the raster around each survey point
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land1,
                             max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian",
                             verbose = FALSE)
```

Density at each point depends on habitat weighted with a Gaussian kernel of
sigma = 250 m, the true scale of effect. The comments give the other true
values.

```{r simulate}
# Habitat smoothed at the true scale, then standardized (mean 0, SD 1)
land1_250 <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = land1, sigma = 250,
                                 kernel = "gaussian", verbose = FALSE)
hab_true  <- as.numeric(scale(terra::extract(land1_250, pts, ID = FALSE)[, 1]))

sim <- sim_dat_gdr(
  density          = exp(log(400) + 0.5 * hab_true),  # birds per square km
  distance_scale   = 40,                # half-normal detection scale (m)
  removal          = 0.2,               # chance per minute of a first detection
  dist_breaks      = c(0, 25, 50, 75),  # three bands within a 75 m radius
  interval_lengths = c(2, 3, 5),        # a 10-minute count in three intervals
  interval_units   = "minutes",
  site_covs        = kernel_inputs$kernel_dat,   # covariates for the model
  event_keys       = data.frame(survey = paste0("pt", 1:100)),
  seed             = 2
)
umf <- sim$observed              # the unmarkedFrameGDR to analyze

head(umf@yDistance, 3)           # birds by distance band
head(umf@yRemoval, 3)            # the same birds by time interval
sim$truth[1:3, c("expected_density", "expected_abundance",
                 "realized_abundance", "realized_observed")]
```

**How to read the output:** Each row is one survey point. The first two tables
are the data an observer would hand you, and their row totals match. The third
table is the truth behind them. `expected_density` is in birds per square
kilometer. Multiplying it by the area of the 75 m circle (0.0177 square
kilometers) gives `expected_abundance`, the expected number of birds in the
circle. `realized_abundance` is the number simulated there, and
`realized_observed` is the number detected. Under these settings an observer
detects about `r round(100 * sim$truth$observation_probability[1])`% of the
birds present.

# Prepare your own records

## Turn bird records into the two count tables

Field data usually arrive as one record per bird. `prepare_gdr_histories()`
converts those records to the two tables. It finds each bird's first detection
before it applies the survey radius, so a bird first detected beyond the radius
does not enter the count when it later moves closer.

```{r histories}
# Where each column of the record matrix sits: 2 time intervals by 3 distance
# bands (0-25 m, 25-75 m, and beyond the 75 m radius)
cell_map <- expand.grid(interval = 1:2, distance_bin = 1:3)
cell_map$column <- paste0("cell", 1:6)

# One row per bird, with a 1 where the bird was recorded
records <- matrix(0, nrow = 3, ncol = 6, dimnames = list(NULL, cell_map$column))
records[1, "cell1"] <- 1                 # interval 1, 0-25 m
records[2, "cell4"] <- 1                 # interval 2, 25-75 m
records[3, c("cell5", "cell2")] <- 1     # beyond 75 m first, then 0-25 m

linked <- prepare_gdr_histories(
  histories    = records,
  history_keys = data.frame(survey = c("a", "a", "b"),
                            bird   = c("one", "two", "one")),
  event_keys   = data.frame(survey = c("a", "b", "c")),   # every survey done
  event_id = "survey", individual_id = "bird", cell_map = cell_map,
  dist_breaks = c(0, 25, 75, Inf), radius = 75, units_in = "m",
  interval_lengths = c(5, 5), interval_units = "minutes",
  surveyed = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)         # survey c found no birds
)

linked$first[, c(".history_row", "first_interval", "first_distance_bin",
                 "status")]
linked$yDistance
linked$yRemoval

# The two tables go straight into an unmarked frame
toy_umf <- unmarked::unmarkedFrameGDR(
  yDistance = linked$yDistance, yRemoval = linked$yRemoval,
  dist.breaks = c(0, 25, 75), unitsIn = "m", period.lengths = c(5, 5)
)
```

**How to read the output:** `first` has one row per bird and `status` says what
happened to it. The two birds at survey `a` are kept. The bird at survey `b`
was first detected beyond 75 m, so it is left out, and survey `b` becomes a
count of zero. Survey `c` was completed with no birds, which is also a zero.
Mark a point that nobody visited with `surveyed = FALSE`, and its counts become
missing instead.

## Check that the records line up with the surveys

`validate_unmarked_data()` checks a frame against a table of survey
identifiers before you fit anything.

```{r validate}
checked <- validate_unmarked_data(
  object = umf, event_keys = sim$event_keys, event_id = "survey",
  interval_units = "minutes",
  effort = rep(10, 100)               # minutes surveyed at each point
)
checked$valid                         # TRUE: no errors were found
nrow(checked$findings)                # number of errors and warnings
```

**How to read the output:** `valid` is `TRUE` when the check finds no errors,
such as a survey identifier used twice or distance and removal totals that
disagree. `findings` lists each problem with the survey it belongs to. Supply
`effort` so that a count of zero from a completed survey is not confused with a
survey that never took place.

## Add covariates for the time intervals

A removal formula reads its covariates from a table with one row per survey and
time interval. `expand_gdr_intervals()` copies the site covariates you name
into that table and adds the interval number.

```{r intervals}
umf_obs <- umf
# Who ran each count: a covariate recorded once per survey
unmarked::siteCovs(umf_obs)$observer <- factor(rep(c("Ann", "Bob"), times = 50))

expanded <- expand_gdr_intervals(
  object = umf_obs, event_keys = sim$event_keys, event_id = "survey",
  interval_units  = "minutes",
  site_covariates = c(rem_observer = "observer")   # new name = source column
)
head(unmarked::obsCovs(expanded$data), 4)
```

**How to read the output:** The first survey now has three rows, one for each
interval. With `expanded$data` as the model data, `removalformula =
~ rem_observer` lets the removal probability differ between observers, and
`~ I(interval == 1)` lets the first interval differ from the rest. Give the
copy a new name, as here. A landscape covariate whose scale you estimate must
not share its name with a column in this table. For covariates that change from
one interval to the next, use `prepare_gdr_intervals()`.

# Estimate the scale of effect

## Fit a starting model

Start with the model you intend to optimize, fitted with
`unmarked::gdistremoval()`. Its landscape covariate comes from
`kernel_inputs$kernel_dat`, which `sim_dat_gdr()` stored in `siteCovs` above.

```{r fit-mod}
mod <- unmarked::gdistremoval(
  lambdaformula   = ~ land1,      # density depends on the landscape covariate
  removalformula  = ~ 1,          # one removal probability
  distanceformula = ~ 1,          # one distance scale
  data     = umf,
  keyfun   = "halfnorm",          # half-normal detection function
  mixture  = "P",                 # Poisson abundance
  output   = "density",           # report density instead of abundance
  unitsOut = "kmsq",              # birds per square km
  K        = 60,                  # largest abundance considered at a point
  starts   = c(log(400), 0, log(40), qlogis(0.2))  # link-scale starting values
)
```

**Choosing `K` and `starts`:** `K` is the largest number of birds the
likelihood considers at one point. Set it well above the largest plausible
abundance. The most birds present at any point in this simulation is
`r max(sim$truth$realized_abundance)`. The starting values follow the order of
the coefficients, here the density intercept, the `land1` effect, the distance
scale, and the removal probability, each on its link scale. They are optional,
but supply them when you can. One trial data set for this vignette, fitted
without them, returned a distance scale of tens of thousands of meters. Check
that the distance scale is a plausible number of meters before you continue.

## Run the optimizer

```{r optim}
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod    = mod,
                        kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs,
                        n_cores       = 1,
                        verbose       = FALSE)
```

The optimizer refits the whole distance-removal model at each candidate sigma,
which takes 10 to 20 seconds here.

# Read the results

## Read the scale of effect

```{r summary}
summary(opt)
```

**How to read the `summary()` output:** The first two blocks are the same as
for any `multiScaleR` fit. The estimated sigma for `land1` is
`r round(summary(opt)$opt_scale["land1", "Mean"])` m, and a Gaussian kernel of
that width holds 90% of its weight within
`r round(kernel_dist(opt)["land1", "Mean"])` m of a survey point. The fitted
model summary then has one block per component, labeled with its link scale.

## Read the abundance, removal, and distance components

`unmarked::predict()` returns each component on its natural scale.

```{r components}
fit <- opt$opt_mod                 # the model refitted at the estimated scale

dens <- unmarked::predict(fit, type = "lambda")   # one row per survey point
dsig <- unmarked::predict(fit, type = "dist")     # one row per survey point
prem <- unmarked::predict(fit, type = "rem")      # one row per point and interval

# First survey point
rbind(density = dens[1, ], distance = dsig[1, ], removal = prem[1, ])

# Turn the two detection components into probabilities for a 10-minute count
p_near  <- 2 * dsig$Predicted[1]^2 / 75^2 *
  (1 - exp(-75^2 / (2 * dsig$Predicted[1]^2)))    # average over the 75 m circle
p_heard <- 1 - (1 - prem$Predicted[1])^10         # detected at least once
round(c(distance = p_near, removal = p_heard, both = p_near * p_heard), 2)
```

**How to read the output:** The `density` row is in birds per square kilometer.
Multiply by 0.0177 to get expected birds in the 75 m circle, about
`r round(dens$Predicted[1] * pi * 0.075^2, 1)` at this point. The `distance`
row is the scale of the half-normal detection function, in meters. Averaged
over the circle, that scale gives a `r round(100 * p_near)`% chance of
detecting a bird that reveals itself. The `removal` row is the chance per
minute that a bird present is first detected, or `r round(100 * p_heard)`% over
ten minutes. Their product, about `r round(100 * p_near * p_heard)`%, is the
share of birds an observer records. The standard errors and limits in these
rows treat the estimated sigma as known.

Because the data are simulated, you can compare the estimates with the truth.

```{r truth-table}
est     <- summary(opt)$opt_scale                    # sigma and 95% limits (m)
b       <- unmarked::coef(fit)                       # link-scale coefficients
ci_lam  <- unmarked::confint(fit, type = "lambda")   # Wald limits, log scale
ci_dist <- unmarked::confint(fit, type = "dist")     # log scale
ci_rem  <- unmarked::confint(fit, type = "rem")      # logit scale

check <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Scale of effect, sigma (m)", "Density at average habitat",
                "Effect of land1 (log scale)", "Distance scale (m)",
                "Removal probability per minute"),
  Truth     = c(250, 400, 0.5, 40, 0.2),
  Estimate  = c(est[1, "Mean"], exp(b[1]), b[2], exp(b[3]), plogis(b[4])),
  Lower     = c(est[1, "2.5%"], exp(ci_lam[1, 1]), ci_lam[2, 1],
                exp(ci_dist[1, 1]), plogis(ci_rem[1, 1])),
  Upper     = c(est[1, "97.5%"], exp(ci_lam[1, 2]), ci_lam[2, 2],
                exp(ci_dist[1, 2]), plogis(ci_rem[1, 2]))
)
# Does each 95% interval contain the value used to simulate the data?
check$Covered <- check$Truth >= check$Lower & check$Truth <= check$Upper
knitr::kable(check, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

**How to read the table:** Density is back-transformed with `exp()` and the
removal probability with `plogis()`, while the `land1` effect stays on the log
scale. Its estimate of `r round(b[2], 2)` means that a one standard deviation increase
in kernel-weighted habitat multiplies density by `r round(exp(b[2]), 2)`.
`Covered` is `TRUE` when the 95% interval contains the true value. A single
simulated data set shows what recovery looks like. It cannot show that the
intervals are reliable in general.

> **What this means for your study.** Report density with its units and the
> survey radius, and report the effective distance for the scale of effect.
> Say that the coefficient intervals are conditional on the estimated scale.
> `vignette("v09-estimates-and-intervals", package = "multiScaleR")` explains what that
> leaves out.

## Plot the kernel and the density response

```{r plot-kernel, fig.cap = "***Kernel weight against distance for `land1`.***"}
plot(opt)
```

```{r marginal, fig.cap = "***Estimated density across the observed range of kernel-weighted `land1`.***"}
plot_marginal_effects(opt, type = "lambda",
                      ylab = "Density (birds per square km)")
```

**How to read these plots:** The first plot shows how the weight given to a
raster cell declines with distance from the survey point. The dashed line marks
the radius that holds 90% of the kernel weight, and the gray band is its 95%
confidence interval. The second plot shows density across the kernel-weighted
proportion of habitat. Its band treats the estimated scale as known. Set `type`
to `"rem"` or `"dist"` to plot a covariate in one of those components.

## Map density

```{r map, fig.cap = "***Predicted density, in birds per square kilometer, with survey points.***"}
# Smooth the raster at the estimated scale, standardized as in the model
r_scaled <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = land1, multiScaleR = opt,
                                scale_center = TRUE, clamp = TRUE,
                                verbose = FALSE)

# Density for every raster cell, with its standard error and 95% limits
dens_map <- terra::predict(r_scaled, fit, type = "lambda")
names(dens_map)

plot(dens_map$Predicted, main = "Density (birds per square km)")
points(pts, pch = 19, cex = 0.5)
```

**How to read this map:** Each cell holds the density the model expects for a
count centered there. Detection is already accounted for, so the map shows
birds present and not birds an observer would record. With `clamp = TRUE`,
cells with more or less habitat than any survey point are held at the nearest
observed value.

# Refit from several starting values

A distance-removal likelihood can have more than one local optimum.
`make_gdr_refitter()` builds a refit function for `multiScale_optim()`. At
every candidate scale it fits the model from the starting model's coefficients
and from each extra set of starting values you declare. The search stops with an error
when the best likelihood comes from a fit that did not converge cleanly, and a
record of every attempt goes to `audit_dir`.

```{r refitter, eval = FALSE}
# A second set of starting values, named like the model coefficients
cold <- unmarked::coef(mod)
cold[] <- c(log(300), 0, log(30), qlogis(0.4))

refit <- make_gdr_refitter(model = mod, cold_starts = list(cold = cold),
                           audit_dir = tempfile("gdr-audit-"))

# The same search as before, with every candidate scale fitted from both starts
opt_checked <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = mod, kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs,
                                refit_fn = refit, n_cores = 1)
```

With one extra start the search takes about twice as long. In this example it
returns the same sigma as the default search, 250 m, so the estimate did not
depend on where the coefficients started.

# Model spatial correlation among survey blocks

Counts from neighboring areas are often more alike than the covariates explain.
A random intercept for each block of surveys absorbs that, and
`fit_gdr_response_field()` goes one step further by letting nearby blocks have
similar intercepts. The correlation between two blocks falls with the distance
between them as `exp(-distance / range)`. You supply `range` in map units, and
the function does not estimate it.

The stored example groups the 100 points into `r field$n_blocks` square blocks
and simulates block effects with a range of `r field$range` m. Fit the model
with independent block effects first, then pass it to
`fit_gdr_response_field()` with a second set of starting values. The simulated
landscape has no real location, so the EPSG code below is a placeholder. Use
the code of your own projected coordinates.

```{r field-call, eval = FALSE}
# Template: an independent random intercept for each block (TMB engine)
template <- unmarked::gdistremoval(
  lambdaformula = ~ land1 + (1 | block), removalformula = ~ 1,
  distanceformula = ~ 1, data = umf_blocks, keyfun = "halfnorm",
  mixture = "P", output = "density", unitsOut = "kmsq", K = 80, engine = "TMB",
  starts = c(log(400), 0, log(40), qlogis(0.2), log(0.5))
)

# Extra starting values, named by parameter block and position
cold <- c("beta_lambda[1]"   = log(300),      # log density at average habitat
          "beta_lambda[2]"   = 0,             # land1 effect
          "beta_dist[1]"     = log(30),       # log distance scale
          "beta_rem[1]"      = qlogis(0.4),   # logit removal probability
          "lsigma_lambda[1]" = log(0.3))      # log SD of the block effects
settings <- list(method = "BFGS", se = TRUE, threads = 1L,
                 control = list(maxit = 2500L, reltol = 1e-10))

field_fit <- fit_gdr_response_field(
  model  = template,
  coords = block_xy,        # one row per survey: the center of its block
  crs    = 32617,           # EPSG code of the projected coordinates
  range  = 1500,            # correlation range, in map units (m)
  cold_starts = list(cold = cold), tmb_settings = settings,
  audit_dir   = tempfile("gdr-field-audit-")
)
```

```{r field-results, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(field$compare, digits = c(0, 0, 2, 2, 1, 1), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Model", "Density at average habitat",
                           "Effect of land1", "SD of block effects",
                           "Log likelihood", "AIC"))
```

**How to read the table:** Density is in birds per square kilometer and the SD
of the block effects is on the log scale. An SD of
`r round(field$compare$block_sd[2], 2)` means a block one standard deviation
above average has `r round(exp(field$compare$block_sd[2]), 2)` times the
typical density. Both models estimate the same number of parameters, because
the range is supplied. Their AIC values differ by
`r round(abs(diff(field$compare$AIC)), 1)`, so these data do not favor either
model.

`unmarked::predict(field_fit, type = "lambda")` returns density with the
estimated effect of each survey's block. Add `re.form = NA` to set the field to
zero. That prediction describes a block with no deviation, and it is not an
average over blocks. To estimate the scale of effect with the field in place,
build a refit function with `make_gdr_refitter(field_fit, list(cold = cold),
audit_dir, tmb_settings = settings)` and pass it to `multiScale_optim()` as
`refit_fn` with `n_cores = 1`. A search of that kind took about seven minutes
on data like these. `?fit_gdr_response_field` gives the full requirements.

# Current restrictions

| Not supported | What to do instead |
|:--------------|:-------------------|
| An `offset()` term in the abundance, availability, removal, or distance formula | No alternative yet. Do not drop an offset your model needs in order to proceed |
| Zero-inflated abundance (`mixture = "ZIP"`) with `engine = "TMB"` | Use `mixture = "P"` or `"NB"`. A zero-inflated model without random effects can use `engine = "C"` |
| A scale of effect for a covariate that appears only in the availability formula of a single-visit design, or only in the distance formula with `keyfun = "uniform"` | Those components are not estimated in such models. Put the landscape covariate in a component the model estimates |
| A landscape covariate with the same name as a column in the yearly or interval covariate tables | Give each its own name, for example with an alias in `expand_gdr_intervals()` |
| Intervals that include uncertainty in the scale of effect | Report intervals as conditional on the estimated scale |
| `cross_validate()` for `unmarked` fits | Compare models fitted to the same surveys with `aic_tab()` |
| `sim_dat_gdr()` for negative binomial or zero-inflated abundance, detection functions other than half-normal, or repeat visits | Simulate those designs with your own code |
| `make_gdr_refitter()` and `fit_gdr_response_field()` with other package versions. They require `unmarked` 1.5.2, and TMB 1.9.25 for models fitted with `engine = "TMB"` | Use the default refit in `multiScale_optim()`, which has no version requirement |
| `fit_gdr_response_field()` beyond Poisson abundance, a half-normal detection function, density per square kilometer, one visit per point, a 75 m survey radius, and one random intercept for abundance. The range is not estimated | Fit independent random intercepts with `engine = "TMB"` |

# Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval = FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
library(terra)

# 1. Prepare the kernel inputs
data("surv_pts")
pts   <- vect(surv_pts)
land1 <- rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif",
                          package = "multiScaleR"))[["land1"]]
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = land1,
                             max_D = 1700, kernel = "gaussian")

# 2. Simulate a survey (or build the frame from your own records)
land1_250 <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = land1, sigma = 250,
                                 kernel = "gaussian")
hab_true  <- as.numeric(scale(terra::extract(land1_250, pts, ID = FALSE)[, 1]))
sim <- sim_dat_gdr(density = exp(log(400) + 0.5 * hab_true),
                   distance_scale = 40, removal = 0.2,
                   dist_breaks = c(0, 25, 50, 75),
                   interval_lengths = c(2, 3, 5), interval_units = "minutes",
                   site_covs = kernel_inputs$kernel_dat,
                   event_keys = data.frame(survey = paste0("pt", 1:100)),
                   seed = 2)
umf <- sim$observed

# 3. Check the data
validate_unmarked_data(object = umf, event_keys = sim$event_keys,
                       event_id = "survey", interval_units = "minutes",
                       effort = rep(10, 100))$valid

# 4. Fit a starting model, then estimate the scale of effect
mod <- unmarked::gdistremoval(lambdaformula = ~ land1, removalformula = ~ 1,
                              distanceformula = ~ 1, data = umf,
                              keyfun = "halfnorm", mixture = "P",
                              output = "density", unitsOut = "kmsq", K = 60,
                              starts = c(log(400), 0, log(40), qlogis(0.2)))
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = mod, kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs,
                        n_cores = 1)

# 5. Read the results
summary(opt)                                  # sigma, effective distance, model
fit <- opt$opt_mod
unmarked::predict(fit, type = "lambda")       # density, birds per square km
unmarked::predict(fit, type = "dist")         # distance scale, m
unmarked::predict(fit, type = "rem")          # removal probability per minute
plot(opt)                                     # kernel weight against distance
plot_marginal_effects(opt, type = "lambda")   # density across the covariate

# 6. Map density
r_scaled <- kernel_scale.raster(raster_stack = land1, multiScaleR = opt,
                                scale_center = TRUE, clamp = TRUE)
dens_map <- terra::predict(r_scaled, fit, type = "lambda")
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `sim_dat_gdr()` | Simulate distance-removal surveys and keep the true values |
| `prepare_gdr_histories()` | Turn one record per bird into the distance and removal tables |
| `validate_unmarked_data()` | Check a frame against the survey identifiers and effort |
| `expand_gdr_intervals()` | Copy site or visit covariates into the interval table |
| `prepare_gdr_intervals()` | Add covariates that differ among time intervals |
| `multiScale_optim()` | Estimate the scale of effect together with the model coefficients |
| `plot_marginal_effects()` | Plot a covariate's effect in one component with `type` |
| `make_gdr_refitter()` | Refit from several starting values at each candidate scale |
| `fit_gdr_response_field()` | Replace independent block effects with a spatially correlated field |
| `aic_tab()` | Compare models fitted to the same surveys |
